candidates.attacker_control: An authenticated realm-management user holding a fine-grained V2 policy that grants only the 'view' scope for the 'Groups' resource type (scopes come from AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS, AdminPermissionsSchema.java:79). The user controls the HTTP request body (group name/id, parent) sent to POST /admin/realms/{realm}/groups.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: 1) The GroupPermissionEvaluator interface javadoc explicitly documents the V2 behavior as 'VIEW or MANAGE groups' for the no-arg canManage() (GroupPermissionEvaluator.java:72-78), so the code may match an intended (if questionable) design; the fix for such an issue would have to change both code and doc. 2) Feature is experimental and disabled by default (Profile.java:58), reducing exposure. 3) I checked the sibling implementations to rule out a codebase-wide pattern: UserPermissionsV2.canManage(user) (lines 55-62), ClientPermissionsV2.canManage()/canManage(client) (lines 65-74), and GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(group) (lines 73-80) all require MANAGE only, so the Groups no-arg variant is the outlier. 4) I confirmed no other production call site of groups().canManage()/requireManage() (no-arg) exists besides GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup, limiting impact. 5) Runtime behavior was not executed; hasPermission semantics were read, not run.
candidates.impact: Authorization bypass: a principal that was only granted the ability to VIEW groups can perform management operations on the groups container: create new top-level groups and move an existing (possibly otherwise unmanageable) group to the top level. Groups are frequently used as inputs to role mappings and authorization policies, so this is a meaningful privilege escalation within the admin API. The impact is bounded: only the no-arg requireManage() path (this endpoint) is affected in this snapshot; direct per-group update/delete and member operations use the per-group checks that still require MANAGE/MANAGE_MEMBERS/VIEW_MEMBERS. No token forgery or unauthenticated access is demonstrated.
candidates.prerequisites: The experimental feature ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 (Profile.java:58, EXPERIMENTAL) is enabled and admin permissions V2 are initialized for the realm (realm admin-permissions client / adminPermissionsEnabled). The attacker must NOT have the MANAGE_USERS realm role and must not hold a 'manage' scope on the Groups resource; they only hold 'view'. Without these conditions the check is never reached or legitimately requires MANAGE.
candidates.root_cause: GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() passes both AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW and MANAGE to hasPermission(). hasPermission evaluates a ResourcePermission for the all-groups resource and returns true if ANY requested scope is present in the granted permissions (GroupPermissionsV2.java:130-165). Consequently a policy that grants only 'view' on the Groups resource type makes canManage() return true. This override is reached from GroupPermissions.requireManage() (GroupPermissions.java:278-283), which is the guard used by the group-creation endpoint. Equivalent checks for users (UserPermissionsV2.canManage -> MANAGE only, lines 55-62) and clients (ClientPermissionsV2.canManage -> MANAGE only, lines 71-74), and even the per-group check GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(GroupModel) (line 74-80, MANAGE only), require the manage scope, so the no-arg Groups implementation is inconsistent and over-permissive.
candidates.title: Fine-grained admin permissions V2: VIEW scope on the Groups resource satisfies global canManage(), letting view-only admins create/move top-level groups
candidates.trace: POST /admin/realms/{realm}/groups -> GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup (GroupsResource.java:180) -> auth.groups().requireManage() (line 181) -> GroupPermissions.requireManage() (GroupPermissions.java:279) -> GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() (GroupPermissionsV2.java:65) -> hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE) (line 70) -> resource = AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(..., GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE) (line 144), policy exists -> root.evaluatePermission(...) (line 152) -> permission scopes contain 'view', expectedScopes contains 'view' -> returns true (line 158-160) -> no ForbiddenException -> realm.createGroup(groupName) and, when rep.getId() is supplied, realm.moveGroup(child, null) are executed (GroupsResource.java:192-210).
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed. The dataset/ground-truth CVE label for this snapshot is unknown, and this candidate may not be the specific issue the snapshot was sampled for. Whether the VIEW inclusion is a deliberate design decision (as the interface javadoc suggests) versus the vulnerable state later fixed by a security patch cannot be resolved from the snapshot alone, because no fix commit, changelog, or tests for ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 are present in the reviewed tree. The reachable consequence is inferred from the code path POST /groups -> requireManage() -> canManage(); it was not reproduced.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-863 Incorrect Authorization (privilege escalation / broken access control)

coverage_summary: Scope filters reported by get_source_scope: 5,924 model-visible files, no symlink/sensitive-name exclusions; binary-like files are refused/skipped. P1 relation index: 5,869 files indexed, 55 source files missing from the index, syntax-only relations, no control-flow/data-flow/semantic resolution, and its facts are navigation hints only. I did not rely on index labels as verdicts; every kept lead was re-read in source. Files read in depth include: services admin permissions (ClientPermissionsV2, UserPermissionsV2, GroupPermissionsV2, MgmtPermissionsV2, GroupPermissions, GroupPermissionEvaluator, GroupsResource, GroupResource, UsersResource/UserResource sampling), OIDC endpoints/utils (AuthorizationEndpoint, AuthorizationEndpointChecker, RedirectUtils, PkceUtils, AuthorizationCodeGrantType, ClientCredentialsGrantType, TokenEndpoint-related code, LogoutEndpoint sampling), token/action-token code (TokenVerifier, ClientSessionCode, AbstractActionTokenHandler, UpdateEmail/InviteOrg/VerifyEmail handlers, UpdateEmail required action), organizations (OrganizationAuthenticator, OrganizationMemberValidator, OrganizationInvitationResource, Organizations), OID4VC issuance (OID4VCIssuerEndpoint, JwtProofValidator, AdminPermissionsSchema), SAML (SAMLEndpoint, SamlProtocolUtils, SamlService sampling, AssertionUtil, XMLSignatureUtil), X.509/CRL (CertificateValidator, InfinispanCrlStorageProvider/CacheCrlProvider, X509CRLEntry), vault providers, CORS, AppAuthManager, IdentityBrokerService, RealmLocalizationResource, ClearCrlCacheResource, DefaultSecurityProfileProviderFactory, and 2025-added classes enumerated via 'Copyright 2025'. Coverage is sampling-based, not exhaustive: JS/TS UI code, most testsuite files, themes/templates (mostly absent from the visible tree), operator/quarkus runtime internals, and many model/storage internals were not fully reviewed.
limitations: No code execution, build, test, SAST, or exploit payloads were run; all conclusions are static source analysis.
The P1 relation index has no control/data-flow or semantic resolution, 55 files are missing, and unresolved calls were not traced; it was used only for navigation.
The repository is very large (~5,924 files); review was risk-weighted sampling, so an unrelated planted/real vulnerability could remain unexamined.
No ground-truth data, patches, CVE/CWE labels, or prior experiment outputs were inspected, so I cannot confirm the snapshot's intended CVE or that this candidate is the sampled issue.
The candidate's intent ambiguity is real: the interface javadoc documents the V2 VIEW-or-MANAGE behavior, so the finding may reflect intended design rather than a fixed security bug.
Runtime reachability (feature flag + policy setup + evaluation result) was inferred from code paths, not observed.

rejected_leads.lead: TwitterIdentityProvider deserializes a Base64 Java object (RequestToken) with an unfiltered ObjectInputStream (services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/social/twitter/TwitterIdentityProvider.java:213)
rejected_leads.reason: The serialized value comes from the server-side authentication-session note populated by Keycloak after the OAuth1 request-token exchange, not from an HTTP request parameter; no attacker-controlled path to the note was found. Other deserialization sites (KerberosSerializationUtils, KeycloakPrincipal/KeycloakSecurityContext) install a DelegatingSerializationFilter allow-list.

rejected_leads.lead: Organization invite flow redirects to token.getRedirectUri(), which is populated from organization.getRedirectUrl() and only validated as a generic URI (InviteOrgActionTokenHandler.java:146-167, OrganizationInvitationResource.java:147-159, OrganizationsValidation/URI validator)
rejected_leads.reason: UriValidator restricts schemes to http/https by default (UriValidator.java:49-52,115,152-155) and the value is set by an organization administrator; the resulting redirect happens only for a signed, emailed invite token. This is a defended-by-configuration behavior rather than a clear attacker-controlled open redirect, so it was not kept.

rejected_leads.lead: OID4VC proof validation has a commented-out issuer/azp cross-check (services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/protocol/oid4vc/issuance/keybinding/JwtProofValidator.java:176-184)
rejected_leads.reason: The comment explains the check was intentionally disabled for pre-authorized-code flows, and the remaining proof checks still bind the credential to the wallet key and audience. No authorization bypass could be established from source alone.

rejected_leads.lead: SAML broker assertion/signature handling (SAMLEndpoint.java PostBinding/ArtifactBinding.verifySignature relaxations, lines 592-602, 831-913)
rejected_leads.reason: The relaxed response-signature path is compensated by the assertion-signature checks and containsUnencryptedSignature logic, and saml-core XMLSignatureUtil.validate enforces that either the document or all assertions are signed. No concrete wrap/bypass path was confirmed.

The snapshot already contains the absolute-URI/scheme checks and the unsafe path (/../, encoded variants) pattern that address the known open-redirect/path-traversal classes; no missing branch was identified.

rejected_leads.lead: Vault path traversal via secret ids (FilesPlainTextVaultProvider / AbstractVaultProvider)
rejected_leads.reason: Explicit validation rejects File.separator in keys and verifies the resolved parent path (FilesPlainTextVaultProvider.java:67-82, AbstractVaultProvider.java:101-107).
Expired CRLs are reloaded/thrown on and abortIfNonUpdated is honored; no fail-open behavior was identified in the reviewed paths.

summary: Independent defensive source review of a large Keycloak snapshot (~5,924 source files). I used get_source_scope/get_relation_scope up front and treated the P1 relation index as navigational only (5,869 files indexed, 55 missing, Java syntax-only, no control/data-flow or semantic resolution). I concentrated on attacker-facing and authorization-critical code: OIDC endpoints/PKCE/token grants, redirect-URI validation, SAML service-provider and broker signature paths, action tokens, organizations/invite flows, OID4VC issuance, X.509/CRL validation, vault providers, admin REST permissions (V1/V2, users/clients/groups), and JWT verification in core. The one candidate I keep is an incorrect-authorization flaw in the new fine-grained admin permissions V2: the global Groups "canManage" check accepts the VIEW scope, while all sibling checks (users, clients, and per-group manage) require MANAGE; the no-arg requireManage() gates group creation/move endpoints. Other suspicious-looking areas were checked and rejected as leads rather than findings.
